newsitem.title: UK: UK's Cook joins trek to Moscow at time of friction.
newsitem.headline: UK's Cook joins trek to Moscow at time of friction.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook flies to Moscow on Sunday for two days of talks, hoping to strengthen the new Labour government's ties with Russia despite friction over Bosnia.

Western foreign ministers are beating a path to Moscow to massage bruised relations with Russia at a time of NATO enlargement and an apparent Western crackdown on fugitive war-crimes suspects in Bosnia.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was in St Petersburg on Saturday, Cook will have talks in Moscow on Monday and Tuesday, and German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel will come to the Russian capital on Tuesday.
Cook was the first British cabinet minister to visit Russia since Labour trounced the long-governing Conservatives in general elections on May 1.
He was to discuss NATO and bilateral cooperation when he meets his opposite number, Yevgeny Primakov, and First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov.
British officials said Cook would address Russian unease about NATO's planned expansion by committing Britain to impart momentum to the fledgling Russia-NATO partnership council.

Cook wants the council, set up under a landmark pact signed in May giving Moscow a say in some of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's affairs, to hold its first ministerial meeting in New York in September during the U.N. General Assembly.
"The foreign secretary believes Russia is central to the security of Europe and he wants that body to have real life," one British official said.
Russia bitterly opposed the decision taken at last week's NATO summit in Madrid to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the U.S.-led alliance.
Primakov called it "the biggest mistake in Europe since the end of World War Two".

Moscow had equally harsh words for a NATO swoop last Thursday, carried out by British soldiers, on two Bosnian Serb war crimes suspects, one of whom, prominent police chief Simo Drljaca, was shot dead.
The Russian foreign ministry said such "cowboy raids" threatened the 1995 Dayton peace process. Moscow hinted it could pull out of the NATO-led international peacekeeping force known as SFOR.

But British officials believe the tough talk is for domestic consumption to disarm nationalist critics who say President Boris Yeltsin has done too little to help Russia's fellow Orthodox Slav Serbs in Bosnia.
They hope the issue will not sour Cook's talks.
On the bilateral front, Cook hoped to put the finishing touches to an agreement on closer cooperation between Britain and Russia in the fight against crime, drugs and terrorism.
The pact, involving closer liaison between the two countries' police and intelligence services, is due to be signed by Prime Minister Tony Blair in Moscow this autumn.

Britain, which last month posted a police liaison officer permanently in Moscow, has so far largely escaped the attention of Russia's spreading mafia and ministers hope the cooperation pact will help to keep it that way.
Cook will also spell out his ideas for boosting trade with Russia when he meets British businessmen.
Although exports to Russia last year topped a billion pounds ($1.70 billion) for the first time, Russia ranks a lowly 30th on the list of Britain's trading partners.
